hints: Start by thinking about the normal job of B-lymphocytes - what should they attack, and what should they leave alone?
Now link a failure of that recognition to MG - what type of disease attacks the body's own cells, and which self-antigen at the muscle is targeted?
walkthrough:
Remember Self-Tolerance**
Your immune system must attack foreign antigens but ignore your own proteins. This ability to tell self from non-self develops when lymphocytes mature, and any defective self-reactive lymphocytes should normally be destroyed.

Apply Autoimmunity to MG**
In MG this control fails. B-lymphocytes make antibodies against your own acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic muscle membrane. Because the immune system is attacking self, MG is called an autoimmune disorder of the immune system.

Final answer: MG is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system fails to distinguish self from non-self. Antibodies are produced against self-antigens, the acetylcholine receptors on the muscle cell membrane at the neuromuscular junction.

hints: Think about what every vaccine must contain to be recognised, but here the target is not a pathogen - what cells are the antigens coming from?
Recall the normal sequence after vaccination - how does the body turn antigen recognition into a lasting defence?
Finish the story for MG - what will the new antibodies and memory cells do when the harmful T and B-lymphocytes appear again?
walkthrough:
A Vaccine Against Your Own Cells**
This is unusual because the antigen is not from a pathogen. The vaccine carries antigens characteristic of the defective MG-causing T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes, or their abnormal antibodies, so they look foreign to the healthy immune system.

Trigger Active Immunity**
Macrophages present these antigens and activate specific healthy lymphocytes by clonal selection. Selected B-lymphocytes divide by clonal expansion, with T-helper cells releasing cytokines, to form plasma cells and memory cells. This is active immunity because your own body makes the response.

Destroy and Remember**
Plasma cells secrete antibodies that bind and destroy the defective lymphocytes or the antibodies they make against ACh receptors. Memory cells persist long-term, so any newly produced defective lymphocytes trigger a fast secondary response before they can cause MG.

Final answer: Vaccine contains antigens of the defective T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes. This stimulates an immune response with clonal selection and expansion of specific lymphocytes to form plasma cells and memory cells. Plasma cells secrete antibodies against the defective lymphocytes and memory cells remain to give a rapid secondary response on re-exposure.

hints: Think about what happens when bacteria are widely exposed to antibiotics even when they are not causing disease - what evolutionary risk does this create?
walkthrough:
Cost of Widespread Use**
Antibiotics kill sensitive bacteria but any mutant bacteria that can survive will be selected for. Giving antibiotics preventively to many people without TB symptoms increases selection pressure, so resistant strains such as MDR-TB are more likely to arise and spread.
Final answer: Increases the risk of antibiotic resistance developing in TB bacteria, making antibiotics ineffective.

hints: First convert the 75% statistic into a number of people - how many of the 36.9 million in Fig. 6.1 do not know they are infected?
Use Fig. 6.1 to think about what those unaware people are missing - what treatment reduces virus to undetectable levels and who cannot get it without a diagnosis?
Now link not knowing to two outcomes - what happens to their own health and to the risk for other people in the population?
walkthrough:
Calculate the Hidden Number**
Only 75% knew their status, so $100 - 75 = 25$% did not know. $0.25 \times 36.9$ million $\approx 9.2$ million people are infected but unaware. That is the importance - almost one quarter of the total in Fig. 6.1.

Risk to Themselves**
Fig. 6.1 shows 21.7 million were provided with ART and 47% of those had no detectable virus. People who do not know cannot access ART, so virus is not controlled, viral load stays high, and they have greater risk of progressing to AIDS and dying from HIV-related disease.

Risk to Others and Control**
High viral load plus no knowledge means greater risk of transmitting HIV unknowingly through unsafe sex without condoms, sharing contaminated needles, donating blood, or breastfeeding. This drives new infections shown as 1.8 million in Fig. 6.1 and shows why more testing, education and contact tracing are needed.

Final answer: 25% of 36.9 million = approx. 9.2 million people do not know they are living with HIV. Without diagnosis they cannot access ART, so retain high viral loads with greater risk of developing AIDS and dying. They pose greater risk of transmitting HIV to others, e.g. by unsafe sex, needle sharing, blood donation or mother to child, increasing spread and health-care burden.
